title: The town that turned
hook: only the people of Yunus turned back in time and were spared (10:98)

segments.voice: Yesterday, too late: Pharaoh's right words as the sea closed. Your line was don't wait for the water. Did you do the smallest version of the thing you'd been putting off? Day four hundred thirty-one.

Read the Qur'an's stories of earlier peoples in a row and a pattern shows up. A prophet comes. He warns. The people mock him. The warning comes true. Nuh's people, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lut, Pharaoh. Again and again, the same ending. So when yesterday's story ends with Pharaoh in the water, you might expect the next one to end the same way. Then, a few verses later, Surah Yunus stops and asks a question: why was there no town that believed in time? And it gives one exception. Just one. The town that gives the surah its name.

Verse ninety-eight, in paraphrase: if only there had been a town that believed, and its belief had benefited it, except the people of Yunus. When they believed, God lifted from them the punishment of disgrace in this life, and let them enjoy life for a while. The Qur'an doesn't name the town; many commentators say Nineveh, on the Tigris, the same city named in the Bible's book of Jonah, which Jews and Christians read too. Here's the strange part. In the account many commentators give, Yunus wasn't there for it. Other surahs tell how he went off in anger, fled to a laden ship, and was swallowed by the great fish. The commentators place the town's turning behind him: the people saw the first signs of the punishment, and they went out of the city together, men, women and children, and cried out to God, and turned. And the punishment that was coming was lifted. So in the very surah that holds Pharaoh's too late, there is a whole city that was not too late. The door that closes at the death rattle was still wide open for them, and they walked through it at the last moment, all at once. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once said, in a hadith in Bukhari: don't say I'm better than Yunus son of Matta. The prophet who went off in anger is honored by name, and so is the town that turned behind his back. One verse, and it changes how you hear all the stories around it. The pattern isn't fate. It can break.
screen: `ONE TOWN BELIEVED IN TIME.` · `NINEVEH, MANY COMMENTATORS SAY.` · `YUNUS HAD ALREADY LEFT.` · `THE PATTERN CAN BREAK.` · then, large: `IT'S NOT TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn back from one thing today. Sit, and breathe. Think of a pattern in your own life that keeps ending the same way: the same argument, the same late night, the same thing said too sharply. Picture the moment just before it starts again. Now picture turning, right there, in some small way. If you pray, you can ask God to turn toward you, the way He turned toward the town. The bell holds the time.
Yunus. The prophet whose people, after seeing the first signs of punishment, turned back and were spared, the one exception named in Surah Yunus. Today's word.
Your line: it's not too late. Today, catch one old pattern just before it starts, and turn it, even by a degree. Day four hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Muslim preachers often tell the story of the people of Yunus when calling a community to repentance, as the Qur'an's example of a whole town that turned back in time and was spared.

fork.setup: you live in a city. your prophet warned you, and left. now you see the first signs of what he warned about. what do you do?
options: wait and see if it's real.
go out together and turn back to God.
chase after the prophet and blame him.
fork.reveal: commentators say they went out together, men, women and children, and turned. 10:98 says the punishment was lifted.

original.note: Arabic: "the people of Yunus," the one exception named in 10:98.

trapdoor: what you thought: a footnote to the story of the whale.
what it means: the one town in the Qur'an's warnings that turned back in time, and was spared.
what a scholar hears: 10:98 breaks the 'punishment narrative' pattern of the Meccan surahs; the details of the town's repentance come from tafsir reports, not the Qur'an itself.

sources.ref: Qur'an 21:87; 37:139–148; 68:48–50 (Yunus leaves in anger; the fish)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3395 (don't say I'm better than Yunus son of Matta)

notes: The scene of the town going out together and crying to God is from tafsir reports (e.g. at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir), told here as 'commentators fill in'; confirm.
Bukhari 3395 cited from memory; confirm the number and wording of the paraphrase.
The Qur'an's order of events (whether the town turned after Yunus left, and he returned to them per 37:147–148) is simplified; confirm.
The brief mention of the book of Jonah is meant only as a neighbor's shared story, not a comparison. Confirm.

Audit (y2 10% sample): the teach and a myth stated as Qur'anic fact that Yunus had left before the town turned; the Qur'an tells of his leaving (21:87, 37:140) but the order relative to 10:98 comes from tafsir, so both now attribute it to the commentators. 'Ran from his mission' softened to 'went off in anger', the Qur'an's own description.
